questions.title: When should dexamethasone be given in bacterial meningitis to reduce neurological complications?
questions.question: In a patient being treated for bacterial meningitis, at what point should adjunctive dexamethasone be given to reduce the risk of neurological complications such as hearing loss?

options.A: With or just before the first dose of antibiotics
options.B: Only after 48 hours of antibiotic therapy, once the diagnosis is confirmed by culture
options.C: Only if the patient develops seizures during treatment
options.D: It should never be combined with antibiotic therapy for meningitis

explanations.A: Correct. Adjunctive dexamethasone, given intravenously with or just before the first dose of antibiotic therapy, blunts the inflammatory response generated as bacterial cell walls lyse under antibiotic action, reducing the risk of neurological complications such as sensorineural hearing loss. This benefit depends critically on early, first-dose timing rather than on the antibiotic choice itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dexamethasone started after antibiotics have already been running for some time no longer meaningfully blunts the early lytic inflammatory surge, so delaying it to 48 hours loses most of its benefit.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dexamethasone's role here is prophylactic, given at the start of treatment to prevent complications, not reserved for a specific complication such as seizures once it has already occurred.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adjunctive dexamethasone is a well-established part of bacterial meningitis management when timed correctly, not an agent to avoid combining with antibiotics.

questions.learning_objective: State that dexamethasone is given with or immediately before the first dose of antibiotics in bacterial meningitis, to reduce neurological complications such as hearing loss.

questions.title: Which antipsychotic is preferred for treating psychosis in a patient with Parkinson disease?
questions.question: A patient with Parkinson disease develops visual hallucinations attributed to their dopaminergic therapy. Which antipsychotic is preferred to treat this psychosis with the lowest risk of worsening their parkinsonian motor symptoms?

explanations.A: Correct. Most antipsychotics are potent D2 receptor antagonists that would worsen this patient's parkinsonism. Quetiapine, an atypical antipsychotic with comparatively weak and rapidly-dissociating D2 receptor blockade, is preferred for psychosis in Parkinson disease instead. It controls psychotic symptoms with a substantially lower risk of exacerbating extrapyramidal motor symptoms than typical antipsychotics or most other atypical agents.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Haloperidol is a potent typical antipsychotic with strong D2 receptor blockade, which would markedly worsen this patient's parkinsonism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Risperidone, though atypical, still has relatively strong D2 blockade at clinical doses and carries a meaningfully higher risk of worsening parkinsonism than quetiapine.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chlorpromazine is a typical antipsychotic with strong D2 blockade and prominent extrapyramidal side effects, unsuitable for a Parkinson disease patient.

questions.learning_objective: State that quetiapine is preferred over other antipsychotics for treating psychosis in Parkinson disease because of its low risk of worsening parkinsonian motor symptoms.

questions.title: Which term describes the progressive decrease in response to a repeated, non-threatening stimulus?
questions.question: A loud but harmless noise repeated many times produces a progressively smaller startle response each time it is presented. Which form of learning does this illustrate?

explanations.A: Correct. Habituation is a simple, non-associative form of learning. The strength of a behavioural response to a repeated, unchanging stimulus progressively decreases as the nervous system learns that the stimulus is neither novel nor threatening and can safely be ignored. This is exactly what is described here, as the startle response wanes with repetition.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Classical conditioning requires pairing a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus to create a new learned association, not the simple decline in response to one repeated stimulus described here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Operant conditioning involves learning an association between a behaviour and its consequence (reinforcement or punishment), not a passive decline in response to a repeated stimulus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sensitisation is the opposite phenomenon — an enhancement, not a decrease, of a response, typically after exposure to a strong or noxious stimulus.

questions.learning_objective: State that habituation is a non-associative form of learning in which the response to a repeated, non-threatening stimulus progressively decreases.

questions.title: Which artery connects the internal carotid artery with the posterior cerebral artery?
questions.question: Which vessel of the circle of Willis links the internal carotid artery directly with the posterior cerebral artery, connecting the anterior (carotid) and posterior (vertebrobasilar) cerebral circulations?

explanations.A: Correct. The posterior communicating artery is a short anastomotic vessel that runs backward from the internal carotid artery to join the posterior cerebral artery on each side. It forms part of the posterior half of the circle of Willis, linking the anterior (carotid) and posterior (vertebrobasilar) cerebral circulations. This anastomosis allows collateral flow between the two systems if one is compromised.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The anterior communicating artery connects the two anterior cerebral arteries across the midline, not the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The anterior choroidal artery is a branch of the internal carotid artery supplying deep structures such as the choroid plexus and internal capsule; it does not connect to the posterior cerebral artery directly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The basilar artery is formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries and supplies the posterior circulation itself; it is not the anastomosis linking it to the carotid system.

questions.learning_objective: State that the posterior communicating artery connects the internal carotid artery with the posterior cerebral artery.

questions.title: Which drug is used for the acute (abortive) treatment of a moderate-to-severe migraine attack?
questions.question: A patient with a moderate-to-severe migraine attack already in progress needs acute treatment to abort the headache. Which drug is appropriate for this purpose?

explanations.A: Correct. Sumatriptan is a selective serotonin 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist, a 'triptan'. It is used for the acute (abortive) treatment of moderate-to-severe migraine attacks once a headache has already started. It works by causing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibiting the release of vasoactive neuropeptides from trigeminal nerve terminals.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Propranolol is a prophylactic migraine agent, taken regularly to reduce the frequency of future attacks, not to treat one already under way.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Amitriptyline is likewise used for migraine prophylaxis, not for aborting a current attack.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Topiramate is a prophylactic antiepileptic used to prevent migraine attacks, not an acute abortive treatment.

questions.learning_objective: State that sumatriptan is used for the acute, abortive treatment of a moderate-to-severe migraine attack, distinct from prophylactic migraine therapy.

questions.title: Which drug is first-line disease-modifying therapy for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis?
questions.question: A patient newly diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis is starting disease-modifying therapy for the first time. Which of the following is a first-line agent for this purpose?

explanations.A: Correct. Interferon beta-1 is given by injection. It is a first-line disease-modifying therapy for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, reducing the frequency of relapses and slowing the accumulation of new demyelinating lesions. This benefit is achieved through its immunomodulatory effects on the underlying autoimmune process.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Natalizumab, a monoclonal antibody, is reserved for patients whose disease remains active despite first-line therapy, or for more aggressive disease, reflecting its greater efficacy but also its greater risk, including progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone treats acute relapses of multiple sclerosis; it is not a disease-modifying therapy used to prevent future relapses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Riluzole is used in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, an unrelated motor neuron disease, not multiple sclerosis.

questions.learning_objective: State that interferon beta-1 is a first-line disease-modifying therapy for multiple sclerosis, distinct from second-line agents such as natalizumab.
